questions.prompt: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?

options.text: Vertical adds resources to one machine; horizontal adds more machines
They are two names for the same technique
Vertical applies to databases and horizontal only to web servers
Vertical adds more machines; horizontal adds more resources to one machine

questions.explanation: Scaling up means a bigger machine, which is simple but has a hard ceiling and a single point of failure. Scaling out means more machines, which scales further but forces you to deal with distribution.

questions.prompt: Why is it important for application servers behind a load balancer to be stateless?

options.text: It guarantees requests are processed in order
It removes the need for a database
Stateless servers use less CPU per request
Any request can be served by any instance, so instances can be added or removed freely

questions.explanation: If session state lives in server memory, a user is pinned to one instance and losing it loses their session. Moving state to a shared store makes instances interchangeable and disposable.

questions.prompt: What does latency measure, as distinct from throughput?

options.text: The total data stored by the system
The number of requests handled per second
The time taken to service a single request
The percentage of requests that succeed

questions.explanation: Latency is per-request time and throughput is requests per unit time. They can move in opposite directions: batching often raises throughput while making each individual request slower.

questions.prompt: Why is p99 latency usually reported alongside average latency?

options.text: It is always equal to the average multiplied by 99
It measures the number of failed requests
It shows the tail of the distribution, which averages hide
It is cheaper to compute than the average

questions.explanation: An average can look healthy while one request in a hundred takes seconds. Since a single page may issue many backend calls, tail latency often dominates what a user actually experiences.

questions.prompt: A load balancer distributing requests using round robin has which limitation?

options.text: It cannot be used with HTTP
It can only distribute across two backends
It requires all backends to share memory
It ignores how loaded or how fast each backend actually is

questions.explanation: Round robin treats all backends as identical, so a slow or overloaded instance still receives its full share. Least-connections or latency-aware policies adapt to real conditions instead.

questions.prompt: What is a single point of failure?

options.text: A bug that appears only once during testing
A component whose failure brings down the whole system
The first server a request reaches
The slowest component in a request path

questions.explanation: Availability is limited by any component with no redundancy. Ironically the load balancer added for redundancy becomes one itself unless it is deployed in a redundant pair.

questions.prompt: What does horizontal scaling of a stateful database make harder, compared with scaling web servers?

options.text: Network bandwidth becomes irrelevant
Data must be partitioned or replicated, raising consistency concerns
Databases cannot run on more than one machine at all
Queries become impossible to index

questions.explanation: Stateless servers can simply be cloned. Data cannot: you must decide where each row lives and what happens when copies disagree, which is why the database is usually the hardest tier to scale.

questions.prompt: In a three-tier architecture, what is the role of the application tier?

options.text: It holds business logic between the presentation and data tiers
It balances load across the database
It renders the user interface in the browser
It stores data durably on disk

questions.explanation: Separating presentation, logic and storage lets each tier be scaled, deployed and reasoned about independently, and stops business rules from being duplicated in the UI.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a reverse proxy sitting in front of application servers?

options.text: To replace the need for a database
To compile application code before it runs
To terminate TLS, route requests and shield backends from direct exposure
To let clients hide their IP addresses from the server

questions.explanation: A reverse proxy acts on behalf of the servers, centralising TLS termination, routing, caching and rate limiting. A forward proxy is the one that acts on behalf of clients.

questions.prompt: A service is described as having 99.9 percent availability. Roughly how much downtime does that permit per year?

options.text: About 8.8 hours
About 3.7 days
About 5 minutes
About 53 minutes

questions.explanation: 0.1 percent of a 365-day year is roughly 8.77 hours. Each additional nine cuts this by a factor of ten, so 99.99 percent allows about 53 minutes.
